title: Satellite and Aerial Imaging in Urban Surveillance: The Overhead Witness
body:
GLMZ's surveillance architecture extends vertically into low Earth orbit through commercial imaging satellite constellations operated by three primary providers under Municipal and Corponation Zone licensing agreements: OrbWatch Industries, SkyLens Meridian, and the Collective Imaging Consortium, a cooperative of smaller operators. Combined, these constellations provide sub-meter optical resolution imaging of the entire city grid on a revisit cycle of approximately 4 minutes for Tier 1 and 2 zones and 22 minutes for Periphery districts. Synthetic aperture radar capability provides imaging through cloud cover and darkness, while multispectral analysis enables detection of heat signatures, surface material classification, and vegetation stress indicators that function as proxies for unauthorized habitation or industrial activity in restricted zones.

The data products generated by overhead imaging are consumed by multiple stakeholder classes. Corporate zone administrators use continuous change detection algorithms to identify unauthorized construction, illicit surface modifications to corporate-managed infrastructure, and encroachment by informal settlements on designated buffer zones. Law enforcement contractors use historical image archives to reconstruct the development timeline of suspected criminal operations — an illicit manufacturing facility's construction, a contraband distribution network's physical infrastructure, or the establishment of an unauthorized community in a restricted zone. The 18-month hot storage and 10-year archive requirements for overhead imaging data in GLMZ mean that the physical history of any surface-visible location is reconstructable with considerable completeness.

The integration of overhead imaging with ground-level sensor networks creates what GLMZ security planners call the Convergent Observation Model, in which any event of interest can be examined from multiple simultaneous perspectives: ground-level optical, acoustic, biometric, and electromagnetic data combined with overhead imagery to produce a comprehensive record that is far more complete than any individual sensor type could generate. This model is most fully realized in Tier 1 corporate zones, where sensor density and data integration are highest, but the overhead imaging component provides meaningful convergent capability even in areas where ground sensor density is low. A gathering in a Periphery district with no LexScan or EmPrint coverage may still generate overhead imagery that documents participant count, vehicle presence, and duration.

The regulatory framework governing satellite imaging of urban populations in GLMZ is notably permissive compared to pre-city-state international norms. Corporate zone sovereignty declarations explicitly include airspace rights that have been interpreted to permit direct contracting for imaging services without municipal oversight. This means that individual corporations can commission targeted overhead surveillance of specific addresses, individuals' home locations, or competitor facilities without any notification requirement or judicial review process. Civil liberties advocates have focused particular attention on the use of overhead imaging to monitor refugee settlement camps in Periphery districts, documenting cases in which image-derived population counts and settlement expansion data have been used to trigger enforcement actions against communities that had no awareness they were being observed from above.
